name: Cis-Sutlej states
native: ਸਤਲੁਜ ਦੇ ਇਸ ਪਾਰ ਦੀਆਂ ਰਿਆਸਤਾਂ (Satluj de is pār dīāṁ riāsatāṁ)

predecessors.name: Sikh Confederacy (the misls)
predecessors.text: Sirhind and the country between the Sutlej and the Yamuna, handed to Ala Singh of Patiala and the other chiefs after 1764 (the sikh-confederacy 1764 keyframe), up to the confederacy's end in 1799

successors.name: British Empire in India (East India Company rule)
successors.text: the land 'between the Sutlej River on the north, the Himalayas on the east' and 'the Yamuna River and Delhi District on the south', Sirsa District on the west: Patiala, Jind, Nabha, Kaithal, Kalsia…

ledger.x: 1800: the Phulkian and other Sikh chiefs between the Sutlej and the Yamuna stand on their own after the Sikh Confederacy ends.
26 July 1806: Ranjit Singh crosses the Sutlej and takes Ludhiana.
1808: Ranjit Singh's third expedition takes Ambala and Faridkot.
25 April 1809: Ranjit Singh gives Ambala and Faridkot back.
25 April 1809: the Treaty of Amritsar ends the Sikh Empire's push south of the Sutlej and puts the Cis-Sutlej chiefs under British protection.
29 July 1809: Ochterlony recognises Ranjit Singh's hold on the south bank of the Sutlej from Chamkaur to Harike Patan, 'and other chiefs received villages as rewards'.
1849: the Cis-Sutlej commissionership joins the new Punjab Province.

certainty.note: The page names bounds and states but no lines: the Sutlej and the Yamuna are the only fixed edges; the inner boundaries between chiefs are not given and the region is drawn from Cliopatria's British Empire step.

Sharp only along the Sutlej, fixed by the Treaty of Amritsar (25 April 1809) and the 1809 recognition of Ranjit Singh's strip; the Yamuna and Delhi District edge and the lines between the Phulkian chiefs and the British districts remain…
